s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:55 PM · OCEAN ROAD → ST. BRENDAN’S — THE LIGHT IS ON
body: Down from Delgado the streetlights on Ocean Road come one to a block, and between them the dark is the real kind: eucalyptus, somebody’s woodsmoke, the sea off to the right somewhere below the bluffs, louder than it looks. Jack has the Carhartt zipped to the collar. Behind him 412 is full of people planning a birthday eleven days early. Ahead of him the A-frame comes up out of the dark with the olive tree leaning over the courtyard wall, a boat somebody turned over on the hill and forgot to come back for.

At the back of the nave, behind the blue glass, the bulb over the closet door is lit. It’s a forty-watt in a wire cage, the kind Pop has over the garage side door on Glenwood, and it means one thing. *Eight o’clock*, Osei said at noon, with the candles still crossed under Jack’s chin.

He has it ready. He’s had it ready since the wax came away from his throat: the red light on State Street and the song, and what that was and what it wasn’t; Sunday, and the bath, and her bed, and one word he let stand in the dark. He could say all of it on the steps without stopping for breath. He knows what the man on the far side of the linen will want at the end of it, too, because it’s what the sacrament wants at the end of everything, and any second-grader at St. Brigid’s could tell you what it is.

At the foot of the steps a sprinkler hisses across the last of the parish lawn and wets the sidewalk in a half circle and starts back. The courtyard gate has been propped open with a brick. Somebody has thought of everything.

choices.key: Wednesday at eight the light over the confessional was on. You walked past it.

s11a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE BOX
body: The card table inside the doors is bare tonight, no lamp and no binder and no Mrs. Fitch, and the nave is dark to the altar. On the closet door the index card still says KNOCK (GENTLY) in her hand, and under it, on a length of string, somebody has thumbtacked a golf pencil, in case a person needs to write it all down first. He stands in front of it with his hand up. He knocks gently. On the far side the beads stop.
Inside it’s the closet: the kneeler, the linen, the coat hooks from 1962. The vinyl on the kneeler has split at one corner since last week, and a little yellow foam shows under his left knee.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been a week since my last confession.”
“A week.” The chair on the far side takes Osei’s weight. “And five minutes early. My mother used to say that a man who comes early to the house is carrying bad news or good fish. Which is it?”
“Probably both, Father.”
“The news first, then. Fish keeps.”
He starts with the song, because it’s the easy one, and it turns out not to be.

“Tuesday I was in a car with Skye. Her car, top down, at a red light on State Street. A song came on the radio and we sang it to each other. All of it, at the top of our lungs.” The linen moves a little with somebody breathing on the other side of it. “It’s about sex, Father. That’s all it’s about. It isn’t even a little bit about anything else. It’s called —”
“I know what it is called.” A pause of a very particular quality. “Mrs. Fitch’s grandson has very good speakers.”
Jack shuts his eyes. Out in the courtyard the sprinkler comes around and goes away again.

“A girl in the next lane filmed it,” he says. “It’s on the internet. My mother’s parish kitchen has seen it. I didn’t mean anything wrong by it, Father, I’m not going to tell you I did. It was the best two minutes of my week, and I didn’t think about it for one second of them.” He finds the rest where he left it, on the walk down. “I’ve been coming in here since before Christmas about one thing. I keep telling you it matters. And Tuesday I sang it like a joke, at a stoplight, with a medal on, where anybody could see. It makes the thing smaller. For me, and for her, and for every kid with a phone who watched a guy who goes to Mass do it. It makes it easier to laugh at.” He doesn’t make it bigger than that, or smaller. “It’s venial. I know it is. It’s a venial sin with about forty thousand people watching.”

“When I was a houseman at Korle-Bu,” Osei says, “there was a drug we gave for everything. Every cough, every fever, every man who wanted to go home with something in his hand. By the time I left, it worked on nobody.” The beads click once. “Words are like that, Jack. The good ones and the holy ones most of all. Give them out for everything and they will do nothing on the day you need them. And people watch you now, because of her and because of that medal. They learn from the people they watch what is allowed to be funny. Sing in the car. Choose the song.”
“Yes, Father.”
“And the fish.”
“Sunday,” Jack says.

He tells it to the linen in short words. “Sunday I received at the eleven-thirty. She came. She knelt. Sunday night I was at her house. A bath, and then her bed. Everything but the one thing, and further than it’s ever gone.” The foam gives under his knee. “She asked me for the one thing first. Before any of it, at the top of her stairs, straight out. I said no. I said *for now*.” He makes himself say the last of it. “After, she said *when*. I didn’t correct her.” And because it belongs on the kneeler with the rest: “I haven’t gone up since. Not Tuesday, not today.”
On the other side the beads go once around something and stop.
“She knows you are here tonight?”
“She told me to come. She said I have to tell you I won’t do it again.” He hears how it sounds, a girl in a bed explaining the sacrament to him, and says the rest anyway. “She said that’s the rule.”
Behind the linen there is a sound that, anywhere but here, would be a laugh. “She has the catechism right. Half my confirmation class does not.”

“Before Christmas,” Osei says, “you knelt where you are kneeling, and I told you that you were not avoiding the occasion. You were scheduling it.” The chair creaks. “You have improved. Now you have a timetable. Sunday at the altar. Sunday night down the hill. Wednesday up the hill to me, and then down again. I have walked it. It is downhill all the way from my door to hers. You are not avoiding the near occasion, Jack. You are commuting to it.”

Jack’s face is hot in the dark. There’s a joke lining up in him about the bus schedule, he can feel it coming around the corner, and it doesn’t survive the linen. He doesn’t argue either. There’s nothing in it to argue with.

“You may come every Wednesday of your life,” Osei says, more gently. “I will be in this chair for every one of them; that is what the chair is for. But I would like, one Wednesday, to see you come up this hill from somewhere else.”
“I am not asking you to know the future. Men fall. I am asking what you intend.” The voice behind the linen is quiet and not soft at all. “Do you mean to stay out of that bed?”

He has had an answer for every other thing he carried in here. He looks for this one and finds two of them: the one Osei is owed, and the one that’s true. Down the hill there’s a girl with a car coming for her at six on Saturday morning, and tonight he isn’t sure they’re the same answer.

choices.text: *Tell him you mean to — and mean it.*
choices.key: Behind the screen Father Osei asked what you intend. You told him you mean to stay out of that bed, and meant it. He absolved you.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything. St. Blaise: two crossed candles at my throat, and then, for me, eight o’clock. Wednesday night I went in. I told him the song, all of it, and Sunday night. He said I’m not avoiding the near occasion, I’m commuting to it. He didn’t ask me to know the future. He asked what I intend. I told him I intend to stop. He absolved me.

response: “Yes, Father.” It’s out of him before he’s tested it, so he tests it after, on the kneeler, like a step in the dark, and it takes his weight. “I mean to. I mean to stay out of it.”
“Good.” The beads go still. “Then make a good act of contrition.”

He says the one from St. Brigid’s, the one with *Thee* in it, at the speed he learned it at seven. When he comes to *I firmly resolve, with the help of Thy grace*, he doesn’t have to slow down and look for it. It’s right there where it belongs.

On the linen Osei’s hand rises in shadow. “…through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son” — the shadow goes down the linen and across it — “and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“For your penance, a decade. The Presentation. Slowly. The old man in the temple waited his whole life; he will not mind waiting for you.” A breath. “Go in peace.”
“Thanks be to God.”

The side door lets him out into the courtyard. The air off the water has turned while he was inside, salt and wet olive leaves and cut grass, and his knee carries the print of the split vinyl into it. Behind him, through the blue glass, the bulb over the closet door is still lit for whoever’s next.

choices.text: *Tell him the truth: you don’t know that you do.*
choices.cue: Father Osei heard all of it.
choices.key: Behind the screen Father Osei asked what you intend. You told him the truth: you don’t know that you mean to stop. He couldn’t absolve you. He blessed you instead, and said the light is on Wednesdays.

response: “I don’t know, Father.” He shifts on the kneeler. “I want to say yes. I walked down here to say yes. I don’t know that I mean it.”
It goes quiet through the linen, quiet enough that he hears a car go by on Ocean Road and take its radio with it down the hill.
“Then I can’t give you absolution tonight.” Osei’s voice hasn’t changed at all. “Not because I don’t want to. It isn’t mine to give to a man who hasn’t decided to put the thing down.”
“I know.”

“I know you know.” The chair creaks. “That is why you came. A man who didn’t know would have said yes and gone home light.” Something moves behind the linen. “You may have a blessing. Anyone may have a blessing. I have given them to dogs.” The shadow of the hand. “May almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“Come back when you can say it. I’ll be here. The light is on Wednesdays.”

On the far side the beads start up again, unhurried, for whoever’s next. Jack stays on the kneeler in the dark of the closet until the split vinyl has printed itself into his knee. At the doors he looks back down the nave. The bulb is still lit.

body: He doesn’t go up the steps.

From the sidewalk the bulb shows through the blue glass at the back of the nave, small and yellow, one caged light over one door in a dark church. The sprinkler comes around and wets his shoes and goes back. The bulb is still on, and Jack is still on the sidewalk.

He could do all of it. He ran it on the way down from Delgado and it’s in order, kind and number: the red light and the song and what that is, which is small and is still something; Sunday, and the bath, and her bed, and *when* left standing in the dark with nobody correcting it. He’d get through every word of that. Osei would hear it out with the beads going. And at the end Osei would ask him the last thing, the one everything else in there hangs on, the line he’s been saying since he was seven, and Jack would have to answer it through a piece of linen, out loud, to a man he respects.

He knows what he’d say. He’d say yes, because yes is the answer that goes there, and Osei would take it, because a priest takes what you hand him through the screen. And Jack would walk out light and down the hill carrying a yes he never checked. He has said a lot of easy things to a lot of people. He isn’t going to say one through that linen.

Four hours ago on the Commons lawn, with a dog sitting on his shoe, his mother said *It’s Wednesday, Jackie*, and he heard her. It is Wednesday. He is on the sidewalk in front of the light. Hearing her got him this far.
A man in a bike helmet comes up Ocean Road on a ten-speed and locks it to the handrail, and stops with one foot on the bottom step when he sees Jack standing there. “You in line?”
“No,” Jack says. “Go ahead.”
The man takes the steps two at a time with the helmet still on, and the door lets him into the dark and closes. The bulb stays lit for the helmet.

Yesterday there was a card table in that courtyard and a boy in a clip-on tie setting the bulletin on fire. Tonight the table is folded against the wall by the gate, and somebody has hung a kid’s red mitten on the end of it for whoever comes back looking.

Jack puts his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt and walks on, downhill, past the courtyard wall and the olive tree and the end of the parish lawn, where the sidewalk goes dry. At the bottom of Ocean Road the porch light is on at Sol’s, and upstairs, in her window, the Christmas bulbs she never took down are lit end to end. He says a Hail Mary on the way down to them, the red-light kind, fast, under his breath. It’s the one thing he’s sure he can say tonight and mean all of it.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:15 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE SUITCASE
body: Sol’s house is quiet for once. Tomás is out and his stereo is off, and the only thing talking downstairs is the old refrigerator in the kitchen, to itself. Upstairs her door is open and the lamp is on. The suitcase lies open on the floor with its contents climbing back out of it a sweater at a time. A gray sweatshirt hangs over the back of the desk chair. The pages for *Caliche* are spread across the mattress, soft at the fold, her pencil in every margin.
Skye is sitting in the middle of them in the coat from State Street, buttoned to the chin, the big collar up around her ears. “I’m breaking it in,” she says. “It has to know me by Saturday.”

body.text: “Did you tell him?” she says, before he has the Carhartt off.

She nods. She looks at his face for a long time, long enough that he can feel it on his skin, and she doesn’t try anything. She gathers the pages off the mattress, knocks them square on her knee, sets them on the suitcase lid, and pats the place where they were. When he lies down she puts her head on his shoulder, coat and all, and folds her hands on his chest where he can see them, and keeps them there.
“I’m not going to make it hard,” she says into his shoulder. “Friday. I want you to know that now, so you don’t spend two days waiting for me to.”

He tells her from the doorway, with the Carhartt still on. Osei asked him what he meant to do, and Jack didn’t know, and said so, and a priest can’t give it to a man who doesn’t know. He got a blessing instead.
She looks up at him from the pages. “Because of me.”
“Because of me,” he says, and touches his own chest, so there’s no mistaking which.

She gets up off the mattress and stands in front of him in the coat, close, and doesn’t touch him. “I cost you that,” she says. “Tonight. Don’t tell me I didn’t. I was in there with you. I’m in there every Wednesday.” She breathes in through her nose and lets it out. “Go back Saturday. I’ll be on a plane. Nobody will be in the way.”
He tells her from the doorway, before she can ask. He got as far as the steps.
“Because you couldn’t say the last part.”
She looks down at the pages in her lap. Downstairs the refrigerator cuts out, and the house gets quieter by exactly that much.
“I told you I’m not mad at it,” she says.
“I’m a little mad at it.” She doesn’t take it back. She lets him have it. It’s fair.

body: Since breakfast, since Theo turned the laptop around, there’s been an apology in him with nowhere to go. He sits on the edge of the mattress with his elbows on his knees and lets it out.

“I’m sorry,” he says. “About the video. About Cassidy, and the network’s concern, and Corinne on the phone before dawn saying *unfortunate* four times. Your mother at six in the morning.” She opens her mouth and he keeps going. “I’m the one who knew every word. You’ve got a show that pays for a house, and I sang you onto a gossip blog at a red light because I wasn’t thinking about anything but —”

She takes his face in both hands. Her palms are warm from the coat’s pockets. She kisses him slow, and then not slow at all, hard, holding his head exactly where she wants it, the sheepskin collar against his jaw and her knees on either side of his on the edge of the mattress, until there is nothing left in him that was going to finish that sentence. When she lets his mouth go she keeps his face.
“Don’t you ever,” she says, with her forehead nearly on his, “apologize to me for making me happy. Not once. Not as a bit. I won’t have it in the house.”
“Okay.”
“Say it back.”
“I won’t apologize for making you happy.”

“Good.” She pats his cheek twice and sits back on her heels. “Corinne called back tonight to tell me my post was *off-message*. She thinks *the clean version* was about the song. Like I was asking you to learn the radio edit.” She points a finger at his chest. “I wrote it about *you*, Youngstown. You’re the clean version. Your mother knows it, your nonna knows it, the boy who wrote *Brother?* knows it. I wanted all of them to see that I know it too.”
“And the network?”

“The network calls it *the incident*.” She says it the way you’d say the name of a yacht. “I’ve never been an incident. Cassidy’s never even been a misunderstanding. Three seasons, and the worst thing she ever did was a C in chemistry, and she cried about it for a whole episode.” She pulls the collar up over her chin and looks at him over it. “Dell Harlan would’ve sung the dirty version louder. And then she’d have keyed the Camry.”
“So that’s where you keep it.”
“Keep what?”
“The mean. You asked me Tuesday where you keep it.”
She thinks about that with her chin in the sheepskin. “At red lights,” she says. “Apparently.” Her face is pleased about it, and a little scared of it, both at once.

“My mother wants me to do a sit-down,” she says. “One magazine. Soft lighting. I talk about my faith journey.” She does Debbie for half a line, sweet as a pie case: “*Tears optional, baby.*” Back to herself: “I told her I’m going to New Mexico to be mean to a horse.”
She leans across him to the windowsill, gets her iPhone, and sets the alarm for Saturday, 4:45, three days early, and turns the screen around to show him. “So I believe it.”
She lies back on the mattress in the coat with the phone on her stomach, and holds out one hand to him without looking, palm up, like he’s the one with her pencil. “Stay till I’m asleep.”

choices.text: *Stay till she’s asleep. Then walk home.*
response: He stretches out beside her with his shoes still on. She takes the pages back off the suitcase and reads Dell at the ceiling under her breath, and when she elbows him he does HARLAN, low, out of the margin she points at. She’s asleep inside ten minutes, the pages rising and falling on her chest, halfway through telling her father where she wasn’t.

He slides the script out from under her hand and squares it on the suitcase. He turns off the lamp. In the dark the Christmas bulbs over the window are the only light left in the room, and the surf comes up the bluff and in at the open window, louder with the lamp off.

choices.text: *Tell her a bedtime story about the rodent. Then walk home.*
response: “Once upon a time,” he says, in Frank’s voice, “there was a rodent.”
She turns her head on the pillow. “Oh, good.”

So he gives her Phil of Punxsutawney: a groundhog with a union card, works one day a year, full benefits, dental, a pension the size of a Buick. Lives in a heated burrow the taxpayers of Pennsylvania built him. Has had it in for the state of Ohio since 1953 on account of a remark about his weight. This morning he comes out, in front of a crowd and a tuba, looks down, sees his shadow, and sentences everybody between Pittsburgh and Toledo to six more weeks out of spite.
“What happens to Ohio?” she says, mostly into the collar.
“Ohio files a grievance. And a man in a kitchen in Youngstown puts down his coffee, and looks at the TV, and says —” He gives it Pop’s pause. “*Like we needed a rodent.*”

She laughs into the sheepskin, and laughs again at nothing a minute later, on the edge of sleep, and the second laugh doesn’t finish. She’s out, collar up to her eyes, the phone sliding off her stomach onto the sheet.

choices.text: *Kiss her at the door and go home while it’s still a kiss.*
response: He takes the hand and pulls her up off the mattress instead, pages and all, and walks her down the stairs to the front door with the coat still buttoned to her chin. On the porch the air off the water is wet and smells of kelp. She kisses him there, under Sol’s porch light, and he kisses her back, and steps down onto the walk while it’s still a kiss.
“Coward,” she says from the doorway, fondly.
“Yes.”

She doesn’t go in. She stands on the porch in the coat with the collar up and her hands in its pockets, and when he looks back from the corner of Del Playa she is still there, being cold in it on purpose.
